extraction.name: BoolQ
extraction.description: BoolQ is a reading comprehension dataset consisting of naturally occurring yes/no questions generated in unprompted and unconstrained settings, paired with Wikipedia passages and yes/no answers.
extraction.creator: Christopher Clark, Kenton Lee, Ming-Wei Chang, Tom Kwiatkowski, Michael Collins, Kristina Toutanova
extraction.citeAs: Christopher Clark, Kenton Lee, Ming-Wei Chang, Tom Kwiatkowski, Michael Collins, and Kristina Toutanova. 2019. BoolQ: Exploring the Surprising Difficulty of Natural Yes/No Questions. arXiv:1905.10044 [cs.CL].
extraction.rai:dataCollection: Questions were gathered from anonymized, aggregated queries to the Google search engine. Queries likely to be yes/no questions were heuristically filtered based on indicator words and length, and kept if a Wikipedia page was returned among the top five results. Human annotators then evaluated whether the question was good, located an answer-bearing passage within the Wikipedia page, and labeled the answer as yes or no.
extraction.rai:dataCollectionType: User-generated content data, Manual Human Curator
extraction.rai:dataCollectionMissingData: Annotators could mark questions as 'not answerable' if the Wikipedia article did not contain the requested information. The dataset only retained questions that annotators marked as having a yes/no answer.
extraction.rai:dataCollectionRawData: Anonymized, aggregated Google search engine queries and English Wikipedia articles.
extraction.rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: Queries were filtered using a manually constructed set of indicator words ('did', 'do', 'does', 'is', 'are', 'was', 'were', 'have', 'has', 'can', 'could', 'will', 'would') and length thresholds. Only questions returning a Wikipedia page in the top five search results were retained. Unlike Natural Questions, each question was paired with the selected paragraph instead of the full document, and only examples with yes/no answers were kept.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: Annotators labeled question/article pairs via a three-step process: (1) deciding if the question is 'good' (comprehensible, unambiguous, requesting factual information) before seeing the article; (2) finding a passage within the Wikipedia document containing enough information to answer, or marking it unanswerable; and (3) marking whether the answer is 'yes' or 'no'.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: Three authors annotated 110 randomly chosen examples and resolved disagreements by consensus to create gold-standard labels. Answer annotations achieved 90% accuracy against the gold standard; differing cases consisted of six ambiguous or debatable cases and five annotator comprehension errors.
extraction.rai:dataBiases: The dataset exhibits class imbalance, with 'yes' answers comprising 62.31% of the training set. There is a topic skew toward entertainment media (22%) and nature/science (22%), and models trained only on passages show slight correlation with answers.
extraction.rai:dataLimitations: Examples are singly annotated, resulting in an estimated 10% error/ambiguity rate. The task is paragraph-level rather than document-level, and questions depend on the presence of relevant Wikipedia articles.
extraction.rai:dataUseCases: Training, validation, and testing of machine learning models for reading comprehension, natural language inference, and yes/no question answering. The dataset is split into 9.4k train, 3.2k dev, and 3.2k test examples.
